The Laborers in the Vineyard
LAY-bor-ers
noun phrase
From the Greek ergates, “labourer” or “workman,” the hired workers of the Lord’s parable of sovereign grace in the vineyard.

📖 Biblical Definition

The parable of the labourers in the vineyard sets forth the sovereign freedom of God’s grace, which gives not by debt but of His own good pleasure. A householder went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard, and agreed with them for a penny a day; and he went out again about the third, the sixth, the ninth, and the eleventh hours, and hired more, saying, Whatsoever is right I will give you. When even was come, the lord of the vineyard bade his steward give every man a penny, beginning from the last unto the first. They which were hired first murmured, supposing they should have received more; but the householder answered, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny? (Mat 20:13). Take that thine is, and go thy way: I will give unto this last, even as unto thee. The dictionary marks this parable as a rebuke to all murmuring against the freeness of grace. God gives no man less than is just, but to whom He will He gives more, of His mere bounty; and none may charge Him with wrong. The closing words pierce the envious heart: Is thine eye evil, because I am good? (Mat 20:15). So the Scripture teaches that salvation is of grace, not of merit; and that the last shall be first, and the first last, for many be called, but few chosen.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Lord’s parable of the householder who paid all his labourers alike, teaching the sovereign freedom of grace.

expand to see more

THE LABORERS IN THE VINEYARD, the Lord’s parable of sovereign grace.

A householder hired labourers at the first hour and through the day.

At even he gave every man a penny, the last as the first.

The first murmured, but he said, Is thine eye evil, because I am good?

Its lesson is that the last shall be first, and the first last.

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 20:1 — "For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard."

Mat 20:13 — "But he answered one of them, and said, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?"

Mat 20:15 — "Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?"

Mat 20:16 — "So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A parable of Scripture; it teaches the sovereign freedom of God’s grace, which none may charge with wrong.

expand to see more

The labourers in the vineyard have drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Lord’s great parable of free and sovereign grace. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the rebuke it gives to every murmur against the goodness of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives not by debt but of His own good pleasure. He wrongs no man, paying each the wage agreed; but to whom He will He gives more, of His mere bounty, and none may charge Him with injustice. The first labourers murmured at His liberality to the last, and He answered, Is thine eye evil, because I am good? So the parable rebukes the envious heart that would bind grace to merit or seniority, and teaches that salvation is wholly of grace; for the last shall be first, and the first last, and the LORD doeth what He will with His own.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “labourer,” the parable names the workers paid alike to teach the sovereign freedom of grace.

The Laborers in the Vineyard — from the Greek ergates, “labourer” or “workman.”

A householder hired labourers through the hours of the day.

At even he paid every man a penny alike.

The first murmured at his liberality to the last.

He answered, Is thine eye evil, because I am good?

Usage

"Like the first labourers, the murmuring heart begrudges God the freeness of His grace."

"Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?"

"Salvation is of grace, not of merit; the last shall be first, and the first last."
